nodes.name: Proof of The tensor product of linearly independent families
nodes.statement: We will prove the equivalent statement: Let $P, Q$ be two free $R$ modules, $f : P \to M$ and $g : Q \to N$ be two $R$-linear injective maps. Then $f \ox g : P \ox_R Q \to M \ox_R N$ is injective. Let $K$ be the field of fractions of $R$. The map \[ P \ox_R Q \to (K \ox_R P) \ox_R (K \ox_R Q) = (K \ox_R P) \ox_K (K \ox_R Q) \] is injective because $R \to K$ is injective and all the modules involved are flat. The map \[ (K \ox_R P) \ox_K (K \ox_R Q) \to (K \ox_R M) \ox_K (K \ox_R N) \] is injective because all the modules involved are $K$-flat (as $K$ is a field). $P \ox_R Q \to M \ox_R N$ is now a factor of the composition of the two injections above, and is thus is injective.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to injectivity of tensor products of injections of free modules; base change to the fraction field $K$, where flatness makes both maps injective.

nodes.name: Proof of A salient finitely generated cancellative monoid is generated by its irreducible elements
nodes.statement: We do not follow the proof from \cite{Cox_2011}. Let $S$ be a finite minimal generating set and assume for contradiction that $r \in S$ is reducible, say $r = a + b$ where $a, b$ are non-units. Write \[a = \sum_{s \in S} m_s s, b = \sum_{s \in S} n_s s\] for some $m_s, n_s \in \N$, so that \[r = \sum_{s \in S} (m_s + n_s) s.\] We distinguish three cases \begin{itemize} \item $m_r + n_r = 0$. Then \[r = \sum_{s \in S \setminus \{r\}} (m_s + n_s) s \in \langle S \setminus \{r\}\rangle\] contradicting the minimality of $S$. \item $m_r + n_r = 1$. Then \begin{align*} & 0 = \sum_{s \in S \setminus \{r\}} (m_s + n_s) s & \implies \forall s \in S \setminus \{r\}, m_s s = n_s s = 0 \end{align*} Furthermore, either $m_r = 0$ or $n_r = 0$, so $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, contradicting the fact that $a$ and $b$ are non-units. \item $m_r + n_r \ge 2$. Then \[0 = r + \sum_{s \in S \setminus \{r\}} (m_s + n_s) s\] and $r = 0$, contradicting the minimality of $S$ once again. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction with a minimal generating set: a reducible generator $r = a + b$ leads, by cases on the coefficient of $r$, to contradicting minimality or non-unit hypotheses.

nodes.name: Proof of Freeness of group algebras under an injective hom
nodes.statement: Pick a section $\sigma : H / f(G) \to H$ and the unique map $\varphi : H \to G$ such that $h = \sigma(h f(G)) f(\varphi(h))$. We claim that $R[H]$ is isomorphic to $R[G]^{\oplus H / f(G)}$, from which the result follows, as such: \begin{align*} R[G]^{\oplus H / f(G)} & \simeq R[H] \\ \varphi(h) e_{h f(G)} & \mapsto h g e_x & \mapsfrom \sigma(x) f(g) \end{align*} Those two functions are clearly inverse to each other, and the forward map is clearly $R[G]$-linear.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a section of $H \to H/f(G)$ and exhibit an explicit $R[G]$-linear isomorphism $R[H] \cong R[G]^{\oplus H/f(G)}$.

nodes.name: The kernel of a map on direct sums
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be an abelian group generated by a set $S$. Let $A, B$ be arbitrary indexing types and $f : A \to B$ a function. Write $f^\oplus : G^{\oplus A} \to G^{\oplus B}$ the pushforward. Then \[ \ker f^\oplus = \Span\{gX^a_1 - gX^a_2 | g \in S, a_1, a_2 \in A, f(a_1) = f(a_2)\}. \]
assumptions: Let $G$ be an abelian group generated by a set $S$.
Let $A, B$ be arbitrary indexing types and $f : A \to B$ a function.
conclusions: \ker f^\oplus = \Span\{gX^a_1 - gX^a_2 | g \in S, a_1, a_2 \in A, f(a_1) = f(a_2)\}.
nodes.statement_short: The kernel of the pushforward $G^{\oplus A} \to G^{\oplus B}$ along $f$ is spanned by differences of generators over identified indices.
nodes.label: 0-ker-mon-alg

nodes.name: Proof of The kernel of a map on direct sums
nodes.statement: Write $I = \Span\{gX^a_1 - gX^a_2 | g \in G, a_1, a_2 \in A, f(a_1) = f(a_2)\}$ for brevity. Note that we can assume WLOG that $f$ is surjective. Write $\sigma : B \to A$ a section of $f$. Let's prove by induction on $x \in G^\oplus A$ that $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) \equiv x \mod I$: \begin{itemize} \item $x = 0$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(0)) = 0$ \item $x = gX^a$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(gX^a)) = gX^{\sigma(f(a))} \equiv gX^a \mod I$ as $S$ generates \item $x + y$: Assume the induction hypothesis for $x$ and $y$. Then \[ \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x + y)) = \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) + \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(y)) \equiv x + y \mod I \] \end{itemize} Now, for any $x \in G^\oplus A$, \[ x \in \ker f^\oplus \iff f^\oplus(x) = 0 \iff \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) \equiv 0 \mod I \iff x \equiv 0 \mod I \] and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $f$ surjective with section $\sigma$; by induction on $x$, $\sigma^\oplus f^\oplus x \equiv x \bmod I$, so the kernel is $I$.

nodes.name: Proof of Independence of group-like elements
nodes.statement:
Let's prove that any finite set $s$ of group-like elements is linearly independent, by induction on $s$. $\emptyset$ is clearly linearly independent. Assume now that the finite set $s$ of group-like elements is linearly independent, that $a 
otin s$ is group-like, and let's show that $s \cup \{a\}$ is linearly independent too. Assume there is some $c : A 	o R$ such that $\sum_{x \in s} c_x x = c_a a$. Since $a$ and all elements of $s$ are group-like, we compute  egin{align*} \sum_{x, y \in s} c_x c_y x \otimes y & = c_a ^ 2 a \otimes a \ & = c_a ^ 2 \Delta(a) \ & = c_a \Delta\left(\sum_{x \in s} c_x xight) \ & = \sum_{x \in s} c_a c_x \Delta(x) \ & = \sum_{x \in s} c_a c_x x \otimes x \end{align*} By Lemma ef{0-tensor-lin-indep}, the $x \otimes y$ are linearly independent and therefore $c_x ^ 2 = c_a c_x$ and $c_x c_y = 0$ if $x 
e y$. If $c_x = 0$ for all $x \in s$, then we are clearly done. Else find $x \in s$ such that $c_x 
e 0$. From the above two equations, we get that $c_x = c_a$ and $c_y = 0$ for all $y \in s, y 
e x$. Therefore \[c_x x = \sum_{y \in s} c_y y = c_a a = c_x a\] and $x = a$. Contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on finite sets of group-like elements: comparing $\Delta$ of a linear relation with independence of the $x \otimes y$ forces a contradiction.

nodes.name: Galois connection between group algebra and group-like elements
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain, $G$ a commutative group and $A$ a $R$-bialgebra. Then bialgebra homs $R[G] \to A$ are in bijection with group homs $G \to \GrpLike A$.

conclusions: Then bialgebra homs $R[G] \to A$ are in bijection with group homs $G \to \GrpLike A$.
nodes.label: 0-grp-alg-grp-like-gc

nodes.name: Proof of Galois connection between group algebra and group-like elements
nodes.statement: If $f : G \to \GrpLike A$ is a group hom, then we get \begin{align*} R[G] \to A g \mapsto f(g) \end{align*} This is clearly an algebra hom, so for it to be a bialgebra hom we only need to check comultiplication is preserved. We only need to check this on $g \in G$, in which case \[(f \otimes f)(\Delta(g)) = (f \otimes f)(g \otimes g) = f(g) \otimes f(g) = \Delta(f(g))\] since $f(g) \in \GrpLike A$. If $f : R[G] \to A$ is a bialgebra hom, then it restricts to a group hom $\GrpLike R[G] \to \GrpLike A$ by Proposition \ref{0-grp-like-map}. Now use that $\GrpLike R[G] \cong G$ from Proposition \ref{0-grp-like-grp-alg}.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions: a group hom extends linearly to a bialgebra hom (check comultiplication on $G$); a bialgebra hom restricts to group-like elements.

nodes.name: Quotients by binomial ideals
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a Hopf algebra, $H$ be a subgroup of $\GrpLike A$ and \[ I = \langle h_1 - h_2 : h_1,h_2 \in H \rangle \] be an ideal. Then $I$ is a Hopf ideal.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Hopf algebra, $H$ be a subgroup of $\GrpLike A$
conclusions: Then $I$ is a Hopf ideal.
nodes.statement_short: The ideal generated by differences of group-like elements from a subgroup is a Hopf ideal.
nodes.label: 0-grp-like-quot-hopf

nodes.name: Proof of Quotients by binomial ideals
nodes.statement: It suffices to check the conditions of a Hopf ideal on generators. For the comultiplication condition: \begin{align*} \Delta(h_1-h_2) &= \Delta(h_1) - \Delta(h_2) \\ &= h_1 \otimes h_1 - h_2 \otimes h_2 \\ &= h_1 \otimes h_1 - h_1 \otimes h_2 + h_1 \otimes h_2 - h_2 \otimes h_2 \\ &= h_1 \otimes (h_1 - h_2) + (h_1 - h_2) \otimes h_2 \in \bar{A \otimes I} + \bar{I \otimes A}. \end{align*} For the counit condition: \[ \varepsilon(h_1 - h_2) = \varepsilon(h_1) - \varepsilon(h_2) = 1 - 1 = 0. \] Finally, for the antipode condition: \[ S(h_1 - h_2) = S(h_1) - S(h_2) = h_1^{-1} - h_2^{-1} \in I. \]
nodes.statement_short: Check the comultiplication, counit and antipode conditions of a Hopf ideal on the generators $h_1 - h_2$.

nodes.name: Proof of Quotient of a diagonalisable bialgebra is diagonalisable
nodes.statement: Note that $R[G] \xrightarrow f A$ factors as $R[G] \xrightarrow f R[f(G)] \xrightarrow\phi A$, where $f(G)$ is a group by Proposition \ref{0-grp-like-grp}. Since $R[G] \xrightarrow f A$ is surjective, so is $R[f(G)] \xrightarrow\phi A$. Therefore Proposition \ref{0-bialg-bij-of-span-grp-like} applies to $f(G)$ inside $A$, and we get $R[f(G)] \cong A$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $f$ through $R[f(G)]$ and apply the previous proposition to $f(G) \subseteq \GrpLike A$.

nodes.name: Counterexamples over a general commutative ring
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{0-bialg-bij-of-span-grp-like} and Corollary \ref{0-diag-iff-grp-like-span} are false over a general commutative ring. Indeed, let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $G$ be a group. Then the group-like elements of $R[G]$ correspond to locally constant maps from $Spec R$ to $G$ (with the discrete topology), hence they are of the form $e_1 g_1+\cdots+e_r g_r$, with the $g_i$ in $G$ and $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ a family of pairwise orthogonal idempotent elements of $R$ that sum to $1$. So $R[G]$ is not isomorphic to the group algebra over its group-like elements unless $Spec R$ is connected. As for the corollary, a bialgebra of the form $R_1[G_1]\times\cdots\times R_n[G_n]$, seen as a bialgebra over $R_1\times\cdots\times R_n$, is generated by its group-like elements but not diagonalizable.
nodes.statement_short: Over rings with disconnected Spec, group-like elements of $R[G]$ are idempotent combinations, so the bijectivity proposition and the diagonalizability corollary fail.

nodes.name: Separation lemma

nodes.name: Rational cone
nodes.statement: A cone $\sigma \subseteq N_\R$ is {\bf rational} if $\sigma = \Cone(S)$ for some finite set $S \subseteq N$.

nodes.name: The diagonalisable group scheme functor
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a commutative group and $S$ a base scheme. The diagonalisable group scheme $D_S(G)$ is defined as the base-change of $\Spec \Z[G]$ to $S$. For a commutative ring $R$, we write $D_R(G) := D_{\Spec R}(G)$.
nodes.label: 0-diag

nodes.name: Diagonalisable group schemes
nodes.statement: An algebraic group $G$ over $\Spec R$ is {\bf diagonalisable} if it is isomorphic to $D_R(G)$ for some commutative group $G$.
differentia: isomorphic to $D_R(G)$ for some commutative group $G$
nodes.label: 0-is-diag

nodes.name: The diagonalisable group scheme torus over $\Spec R$
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an abelian monoid. Then $D_R(M)$ is isomorphic to $\Spec R[M]$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an abelian monoid.
conclusions: Then $D_R(M)$ is isomorphic to $\Spec R[M]$.
nodes.label: 0-diag-spec

nodes.name: Diagonalizable algebraic groups are those whose coordinate ring is spanned by group-like elements
nodes.statement: An algebraic group $G$ over a field $k$ is diagonalizable if and only if $\Gamma(G)$ is spanned by its group-like elements.
assumptions: An algebraic group $G$ over a field $k$
conclusions: is diagonalizable if and only if $\Gamma(G)$ is spanned by its group-like elements

nodes.name: The diagonalisable group scheme functor is fully faithful
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain. The functor $D_R(G) := G \rightsquigarrow \Spec R[G]$ from the category of groups to the category of group schemes over $\Spec R$ is fully faithful.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a domain.
conclusions: The functor $D_R(G) := G \rightsquigarrow \Spec R[G]$ from the category of groups to the category of group schemes over $\Spec R$ is fully faithful.
nodes.label: 0-full-faithful-diag

nodes.name: Proof of The diagonalisable group scheme functor is fully faithful

nodes.name: Morphisms between diagonalisable group schemes are affine
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $M, N$ be commutative monoids and $f : M \to N$ a monoid hom. Then the map $D_S(f) : D_S(N) \to D_S(M)$ is affine.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a scheme.
Let $M, N$ be commutative monoids and $f : M \to N$ a monoid hom.
conclusions: Then the map $D_S(f) : D_S(N) \to D_S(M)$ is affine.
nodes.label: 0-diag-aff-hom

nodes.name: Proof of Morphisms between diagonalisable group schemes are affine
nodes.statement: $\Spec f : \Spec \Z[N] \to \Spec \Z[M]$ is affine, since it's a morphism of affine schemes. Therefore $D_S(f)$ is affine, as affine morphisms are preserved under base change.
nodes.statement_short: Morphisms of affine schemes are affine, and affineness is stable under base change.

nodes.name: Closed embeddings between diagonalisable group schemes
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $M, N$ be commutative monoids and $f : M \to N$ a surjective monoid hom. Then the map $D_S(f) : D_S(N) \to D_S(M)$ is a closed embedding.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a scheme.
Let $M, N$ be commutative monoids and $f : M \to N$ a surjective monoid hom.
conclusions: Then the map $D_S(f) : D_S(N) \to D_S(M)$ is a closed embedding.
nodes.label: 0-diag-closed-emb

nodes.name: Proof of Closed embeddings between diagonalisable group schemes
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is surjective, the corresponding map $\hat f : \Z[M] \to \Z[N]$ is surjective too. Hence $\Spec \hat f : \Spec \Z[N] \to \Spec \Z[M]$ is a closed embedding. Therefore $D_S(f)$ is a closed embedding, as closed embeddings are preserved under base change.
nodes.statement_short: A surjective monoid hom gives a surjective ring map, hence a closed embedding, stable under base change.

nodes.name: Faithfully flat morphisms between diagonalisable group schemes
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $G, H$ be abelian groups and $f : G \to H$ an injective group hom. Then the map $D_S(f) : D_S(H) \to D_S(G)$ is faithfully flat.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a scheme.
Let $G, H$ be abelian groups and $f : G \to H$ an injective group hom.
conclusions: Then the map $D_S(f) : D_S(H) \to D_S(G)$ is faithfully flat.
nodes.label: 0-diag-faithful-flat

nodes.name: Proof of Faithfully flat morphisms between diagonalisable group schemes
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is injective, $\Z[H]$ is a free module over $\Z[G]$ by Proposition \ref{0-grp-alg-free}, hence the map $\Z[G] \to \Z[H]$ is faithfully flat and so is $\Spec \Z[H] \to \Spec \Z[G]$. Therefore $D_S(f)$ is faithfully flat, as faithfully flat morphisms are preserved under base change.
nodes.statement_short: $\Z[H]$ is free over $\Z[G]$, so the map is faithfully flat, stable under base change.

nodes.name: A subgroup of a diagonalisable group scheme is a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain. Let $G$ be an abelian group. If $H$ is a closed subgroup of $D_R(G)$, then $H$ is a diagonalisable group scheme.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a domain.
Let $G$ be an abelian group.
$H$ is a closed subgroup of $D_R(G)$
conclusions: $H$ is a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.label: 0-subgroup-diag

nodes.name: Proof of A subgroup of a diagonalisable group scheme is a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.statement: $H$ is a closed subscheme of an affine scheme, hence it is affine. By Proposition \ref{0-ess-image-spec-hopf}, write $H = \Spec A$ where $A$ is a $R$-Hopf algebra. The closed subgroup embedding $H \hookrightarrow D_R(G)$ becomes a surjective bialgebra hom $R[G] \to A$ by Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-full-faithful-spec-hopf}. By Proposition \ref{0-is-diag-bialg-quot}, $A$ is a diagonalisable bialgebra and therefore $H$ is a diagonalisable group scheme.
nodes.statement_short: Write $H = \Spec A$ for a Hopf algebra $A$, a quotient of $R[G]$; quotients of diagonalisable bialgebras are diagonalisable.

nodes.name: Diagonalisable group scheme of a torsion group is disconnected
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be an abelian group with an element of torsion $n$. Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $n$ invertible. Then $D_R(G)$ is disconnected.
assumptions: Let $G$ be an abelian group with an element of torsion $n$.
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $n$ invertible.
conclusions: Then $D_R(G)$ is disconnected.
nodes.label: 0-diag-tors

nodes.name: Proof of Diagonalisable group scheme of a torsion group is disconnected
nodes.statement: Say $x \in G$ is such that $x^n = 1$. Then \[e : R[G] := \frac 1n \sum_{i = 0}^n x^i\] is such that $e ^ 2 = e$. We are done by Proposition \ref{0-diag-spec}.
nodes.statement_short: A torsion element $x$ yields a nontrivial idempotent $e = \frac1n \sum x^i$ in $R[G]$.

nodes.name: The split torus
nodes.statement: The split torus $\G_m^n$ over a scheme $S$ is the pullback of $\Spec \Z[x_1^{\pm 1}, \dotsc, x_n^{\pm 1}]$ along the unique map $S \to \Spec \Z$.

assumptions: Let $R$ be a domain.
conclusions: The functor $G \rightsquigarrow \Spec R[G]$ from the category of groups to the category of group schemes over $\Spec R$ is a group isomorphism on hom sets.

nodes.name: Proof of Diag is a group isomorphism on hom sets
nodes.statement: Toddlers and streets by Lemmas \ref{0-full-faithful-diag} and \ref{0-full-faithful-grp-hom}.
nodes.statement_short: Asserted as trivial from full faithfulness of $D_R$ and the hom-set lemma for group objects.

nodes.name: Characters of a group scheme
nodes.statement: For a group scheme $G$ over $S$, the {\bf character lattice} of $G$ is \[ X(G) := \Hom_{\mathsf{GrpSch}_S}(G, \G_m). \] An element of $X(G)$ is called a {\bf character}.
nodes.statement_short: $X(G)$ is the group of group-scheme homomorphisms $G \to \G_m$; its elements are characters.
nodes.label: 0-char

nodes.name: Cocharacters of a group scheme
nodes.statement: For a group scheme $G$ over $S$, the {\bf cocharacter lattice} of $G$ is \[ X^*(G) := \Hom_{\mathsf{GrpSch}_S}(\G_m, G). \] An element of $X^*(G)$ is called a {\bf cocharacter} or {\bf one-parameter subgroup}.
nodes.statement_short: $X^*(G)$ is the group of homomorphisms $\G_m \to G$ (one-parameter subgroups).
nodes.label: 0-cochar

nodes.name: Character lattice of a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain and $G$ be a commutative group. Then $X(\Spec R[G]) = G$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a domain and $G$ be a commutative group.
conclusions: Then $X(\Spec R[G]) = G$.
nodes.label: 0-char-diag

nodes.name: Proof of Character lattice of a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.statement: By Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-full-faithful-diag} in turn, we have \[ X(G) = \Hom_{\mathsf{GrpSch}}(G, \G_m) = \Hom(k[\Z], k[G]) = \Hom(\Z, G) = G. \]
nodes.statement_short: Chain of identifications $X(G) = \Hom(k[\Z], k[G]) = \Hom(\Z, G) = G$.

nodes.name: Cocharacter lattice of a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a domain and $G$ be a commutative group. Then $X^*(\Spec R[G]) = \Hom(G, \Z)$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a domain and $G$ be a commutative group.
conclusions: Then $X^*(\Spec R[G]) = \Hom(G, \Z)$.
nodes.label: 0-cochar-diag

nodes.name: Proof of Cocharacter lattice of a diagonalisable group scheme
nodes.statement: By Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-full-faithful-diag} in turn, we have \[ X^*(G) = \Hom_{\mathsf{GrpSch}}(\G_m, G) = \Hom(k[G], k[\Z]) = \Hom(G, \Z). \]
nodes.statement_short: Chain of identifications $X^*(G) = \Hom(k[G], k[\Z]) = \Hom(G, \Z)$.

nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a torus of dimension $n$ over a domain $R$. Then $X(G) = \Z^n$.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a torus of dimension $n$ over a domain $R$.
conclusions: Then $X(G) = \Z^n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Character lattice of the torus
nodes.statement: Immediate from Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-char-diag}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the character lattice of diagonalisable groups.

nodes.name: Cocharacter lattice of the torus

assumptions: Let $G$ be a torus of dimension $n$ over a domain $R$.
conclusions: Then $X^*(G) = \Hom(\Z^n, \Z)$.
nodes.label: 0-cochar-torus

nodes.name: Proof of Cocharacter lattice of the torus
nodes.statement: Immediate from Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-cochar-diag}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the cocharacter lattice of diagonalisable groups.

nodes.name: Proof of The character-cocharacter pairing is perfect

nodes.name: The image of a torus is a torus

Then the (scheme theoretic) image of $\phi$ is a split torus over $R$ and the maps \[ T \xrightarrow{\hat{\phi}} \operatorname{im}\phi \xrightarrow{\iota} G \] are group homomorphisms, and $\hat{\phi}$ is fpqc. nodes.name: Proof of The image of a torus is a torus
nodes.statement: By fullness of $D_R$ (Proposition \ref{0-full-faithful-diag}), it's enough to handle the case where $T = D_R(H), G = D_R(I), \phi = D_R(f)$ for $H$ a finitely generated free abelian group, $I$ an abelian group, $f : I \to H$ a group hom. Then $\operatorname{im}(f)$ is a subgroup of the finitely-generated free abelian group $H$, hence itself a finitely-generated free abelian group (since free is equivalent to torsion-free for finitely-generated abelian groups, and a subgroup of a torsion-free group is torsion-free).
nodes.statement_short: By fullness of $D_R$ reduce to $\phi = D_R(f)$; then $\im f$ is a subgroup of a f.g. free group, hence free.

nodes.name: Proof of A subgroup of a torus is a torus
nodes.statement: By assumption, write $T \cong D_k[G]$ for $G$ a free abelian group. By Proposition \ref{0-subgroup-diag}, $H$ is a diagonalisable group scheme, say $H \cong D_k(I)$ for $I$ an abelian group. Since $H$ is a closed subscheme, the map $G \to I$ is surjective, so $I$ is a finitely-generated abelian group. Since $H$ is connected, Proposition \ref{0-diag-tors} says $I$ is torsion-free, hence free. Thus $H$ is a split torus.
nodes.statement_short: A closed subgroup of $D_k(G)$ is diagonalisable $D_k(I)$ with $I$ a f.g. quotient of $G$; connectedness rules out torsion, so $I$ is free.

nodes.name: Toric varieties
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be a field. Let $T$ be a torus over $k$. A \emph{toric variety} structure on a scheme $X$ over $k$ consists the following data: \begin{itemize} \item a torus $T$ over $k$, \item a group action $T \times X \to X$ over $k$. \item a dominant open immersion $i : T \hookrightarrow X$ over $k$ that is $T$-equivariant. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Torus morphisms, torus isomorphisms

A \emph{toric morphism} from $X_1$ to $X_2$ is the data of a $k$-morphism $X_1 \to X_2$ and a $k$-group homomorphism $T_1 \to T_2$ that commute with the embeddings $T_1 \to X_1, T_2 \to X_2$ and the actions. A \emph{toric isomorphism} from $X_1$ to $X_2$ is the data of two isomorphisms $X_1 \cong X_2$ and $T_1 \cong T_2$ that commute with the embeddings $T_1 \to X_1, T_2 \to X_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Toric morphisms/isomorphisms are pairs of maps on varieties and tori compatible with the torus embeddings (and actions).

nodes.name: Proof of The diagonalisable group scheme of an affine monoid algebra is an affine toric variety
nodes.statement: The map $D_k(G) \hookrightarrow D_k(M)$ is given by the embedding $M \hookrightarrow G$. We identify $D_k(G) \cong \Spec k[G], D_k(M) \cong \Spec k[M]$ using Proposition \ref{0-diag-spec}. By Proposition \ref{0-loc-mon-alg}, $k[G]$ is a localization of $k[M]$. Therefore the map $\Spec k[G] \hookrightarrow \Spec k[M]$ is an open immersion. This open immersion is dominant since $\Spec k[M]$ is irreducible as $k[M]$ is a domain (Proposition \ref{0-aff-mon-alg-domain}). The group action $D_k(G) \times D_k(M) \to D_k(M)$ comes from pulling back along $D_k(G) \hookrightarrow D_k(M)$ the left action $D_k(M) \times D_k(M) \to D_k(M)$ using Proposition \ref{0-comap-mod}.
nodes.statement_short: $k[G]$ is a localisation of the domain $k[M]$, giving a dominant open immersion $D_k(G) \hookrightarrow D_k(M)$; the action comes from pulling back the monoid action.

nodes.name: Proof of An ideal is toric iff it is prime and generated by binomials
nodes.statement: A toric ideal is prime and generated by binomials by definition. Assume $I$ is prime and generated by $X^\alpha - X^\beta$ ranging over $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$ for some set $S \subseteq M \times M$. Note first that $I$ doesn't contain any monomial. Indeed, $I$ is contained in the kernel of the map $R[M] \to R$ given by $X^m \mapsto 1$. Since $I$ is prime, this means that \[ X^{\alpha + \gamma} - X^{\beta + \gamma} \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I. \] In particular, if $\alpha_1 - \beta_1 = \alpha_2 - \beta_2$, then Since $I$ is prime, this means that \[ X^{\alpha_1} - X^{\beta_1} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_1 + \beta_2} - X^{\beta_1 + \beta_2} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_2 + \beta_1} - X^{\beta_1 + \beta_2} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_2} - X^{\beta_2} \in I. \] Now, we claim that $I = I_L$ where $L \le G$ is given by \[ \Span\{\delta - \varepsilon | (\delta, \varepsilon) \in S\}. \] Clearly, $I \subseteq I_L$. For the other direction, assume $\delta, \varepsilon \in M, \delta - \varepsilon \in L$. Let's prove $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I$ by induction on $\delta - \varepsilon \in L$: \begin{itemize} \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = 0$, then $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon = 0 \in I$. \item If $\delta_1 - \varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 - \delta_2$ and $X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$, then \[ X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \in I \iff X^{\varepsilon_2} - X^{\delta_2} \iff X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = \alpha - \beta$ where $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$, then \[ X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item Assume $\delta_1, \delta_2, \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2$ are such that $X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1}, X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$. Then \[ X^{\delta_1 + \delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2} = (X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1})X^{\delta_2} + X^{\varepsilon_1}(X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2}) \in I. \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Forward by definition. Conversely, primality makes binomial membership depend only on $\alpha - \beta$; show $I = I_L$ for the lattice $L$ spanned by the generator differences, by induction on $L$.

nodes.name: Proof of Y_A is a toric variety
nodes.statement: {\textbf Torus: } Define the torus $T'$ to be the one we get from \ref{1-1-1-group-hom-torus} with quotient map $\pi:T \to T'$. {\textbf Open embedding: } Since both $Y_{\MCA},T'$ are closures of $\Phi,\Phi'$ and $\G_m^n\to\mathbb{A}^n$ is an open embedding we get an open embedding $\iota:T' \to Y_{\MCA}$ such that the map $\phi:T \to Y_{\MCA}$ factors as $\phi = \iota \circ \pi$. {\textbf Dominant: } Since $\phi$ is dominant, so is $\iota$. {\textbf Action: } Since $\G_m^n$ acts on $\mathbb{A}^n$, we get a morphism $a':T' \times_S Y_\MCA \to \mathbb{A}^n$. As $T'\times_S Y_\MCA$ is reduced (TODO add lemma), to show that this factors through $Y_\MCA$ it suffices to check that the image lies in $Y_\MCA$. First, $T'\times_S T' \to T'\times Y_\MCA$ is dominant, since $T'$ is flat and flat base change preserves dominance (TODO add lemma). Since the image of $T'\times_S T'$ is $T'$ we're done for topological reasons. {\textbf Equivariant: } The inclusion of the torus is equivariant, since $\G_m^n \to \mathbb{A}^n$ is.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the toric variety axioms for $Y_\MCA$: torus from the image of $\Phi'$, open dominant embedding, action and equivariance from $\G_m^n$ acting on $\mathbb A^n$.

By Proposition \ref{0-ker-mon-alg} with $G := \Z, S := {1}$, \[ \ker R[f_\MCA] = \Span\{X^\alpha - X^\beta | \alpha, \beta \in \N^s, f(\alpha) = f(\beta)\} = \Span\{X^\alpha - X^\beta | \alpha, \beta \in \N^s, \alpha - \beta \in L\}. \]

nodes.name: Apply the previous proposition: $I \subseteq S$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{0-irred-subset-gen}, $I \subseteq S$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the previous proposition: $I \subseteq S$

nodes.name: Conclude $I$ is finite
nodes.statement: Hence $I$ is finite.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $I$ is finite

nodes.name: Departure from Cox
nodes.statement: We do not follow the proof from \cite{Cox_2011}.
nodes.statement_short: Note that the proof departs from Cox et al.

nodes.name: Assume a minimal generator $r = a + b$ is reducible and expand $a
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite minimal generating set and assume for contradiction that $r \in S$ is reducible, say $r = a + b$ where $a, b$ are non-units. Write \[a = \sum_{s \in S} m_s s, b = \sum_{s \in S} n_s s\] for some $m_s, n_s \in \N$, so that \[r = \sum_{s \in S} (m_s + n_s) s.\] We distinguish three cases
nodes.statement_short: Assume a minimal generator $r = a + b$ is reducible and expand $a, b$ in $S$

nodes.name: Case $m_r + n_r = 0$: $r$ lies in the span of the other generators
nodes.statement: $m_r + n_r = 0$. Then \[r = \sum_{s \in S \setminus \{r\}} (m_s + n_s) s \in \langle S \setminus \{r\}\rangle\] contradicting the minimality of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $m_r + n_r = 0$: $r$ lies in the span of the other generators

nodes.name: Case $m_r + n_r = 1$: forces $a = 0$ or $b = 0$
nodes.statement: $m_r + n_r = 1$. Then \begin{align*} & 0 = \sum_{s \in S \setminus \{r\}} (m_s + n_s) s & \implies \forall s \in S \setminus \{r\}, m_s s = n_s s = 0 \end{align*} Furthermore, either $m_r = 0$ or $n_r = 0$, so $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, contradicting the fact that $a$ and $b$ are non-units.
nodes.statement_short: Case $m_r + n_r = 1$: forces $a = 0$ or $b = 0$

nodes.name: Case $m_r + n_r \ge 2$: forces $r = 0$
nodes.statement: $m_r + n_r \ge 2$. Then \[0 = r + \sum_{s \in S \setminus \{r\}} (m_s + n_s) s\] and $r = 0$, contradicting the minimality of $S$ once again.
nodes.statement_short: Case $m_r + n_r \ge 2$: forces $r = 0$

nodes.name: Choose a section $\sigma$ of $H \to H/f(G)$ and the induced map $\varp
nodes.statement: Pick a section $\sigma : H / f(G) \to H$ and the unique map $\varphi : H \to G$ such that $h = \sigma(h f(G)) f(\varphi(h))$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a section $\sigma$ of $H \to H/f(G)$ and the induced map $\varphi$

nodes.name: Exhibit mutually inverse maps giving $R[H] \cong R[G]^{\oplus H/f(G)}$
nodes.statement: We claim that $R[H]$ is isomorphic to $R[G]^{\oplus H / f(G)}$, from which the result follows, as such: \begin{align*} R[G]^{\oplus H / f(G)} & \simeq R[H] \\ \varphi(h) e_{h f(G)} & \mapsto h g e_x & \mapsfrom \sigma(x) f(g) \end{align*} Those two functions are clearly inverse to each other, and the forward map is clearly $R[G]$-linear.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit mutually inverse maps giving $R[H] \cong R[G]^{\oplus H/f(G)}$

nodes.name: Name the candidate span $I$
nodes.statement: Write $I = \Span\{gX^a_1 - gX^a_2 | g \in G, a_1, a_2 \in A, f(a_1) = f(a_2)\}$ for brevity.
nodes.statement_short: Name the candidate span $I$

nodes.name: WLOG $f$ surjective
nodes.statement: Note that we can assume WLOG that $f$ is surjective. Write $\sigma : B \to A$ a section of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $f$ surjective; pick a section $\sigma$

nodes.name: Induction on $x$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) \equiv x \bmod I$
nodes.statement: Let's prove by induction on $x \in G^\oplus A$ that $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) \equiv x \mod I$: \begin{itemize} \item $x = 0$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(0)) = 0$ \item $x = gX^a$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(gX^a)) = gX^{\sigma(f(a))} \equiv gX^a \mod I$ as $S$ generates \item $x + y$: Assume the induction hypothesis for $x$ and $y$. Then \[ \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x + y)) = \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) + \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(y)) \equiv x + y \mod I \]
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $x$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) \equiv x \bmod I$

nodes.name: Zero case
nodes.statement: $x = 0$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(0)) = 0$
nodes.statement_short: Zero case

nodes.name: Single-term case uses that $S$ generates
nodes.statement: $x = gX^a$: $\sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(gX^a)) = gX^{\sigma(f(a))} \equiv gX^a \mod I$ as $S$ generates
nodes.statement_short: Single-term case uses that $S$ generates

nodes.name: Additivity step
nodes.statement: $x + y$: Assume the induction hypothesis for $x$ and $y$. Then \[ \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x + y)) = \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) + \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(y)) \equiv x + y \mod I \]
nodes.statement_short: Additivity step

nodes.name: Conclude $x \in \ker f^\oplus$ iff $x \equiv 0 \bmod I$
nodes.statement: Now, for any $x \in G^\oplus A$, \[ x \in \ker f^\oplus \iff f^\oplus(x) = 0 \iff \sigma^\oplus(f^\oplus(x)) \equiv 0 \mod I \iff x \equiv 0 \mod I \] and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $x \in \ker f^\oplus$ iff $x \equiv 0 \bmod I$

nodes.name: Induction on finite sets $s$ of group-like elements
nodes.statement: Let's prove that any finite set $s$ of group-like elements is linearly independent, by induction on $s$. $\emptyset$ is clearly linearly independent.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on finite sets $s$ of group-like elements; base case $\emptyset$

nodes.name: Inductive step: adding a new group-like $a$ preserves independence
nodes.statement:
Assume now that the finite set $s$ of group-like elements is linearly independent, that $a 
otin s$ is group-like, and let's show that $s \cup \{a\}$ is linearly independent too. Assume there is some $c : A 	o R$ such that $\sum_{x \in s} c_x x = c_a a$. Since $a$ and all elements of $s$ are group-like, we compute  egin{align*} \sum_{x, y \in s} c_x c_y x \otimes y & = c_a ^ 2 a \otimes a \ & = c_a ^ 2 \Delta(a) \ & = c_a \Delta\left(\sum_{x \in s} c_x xight) \ & = \sum_{x \in s} c_a c_x \Delta(x) \ & = \sum_{x \in s} c_a c_x x \otimes x \end{align*} By Lemma ef{0-tensor-lin-indep}, the $x \otimes y$ are linearly independent and therefore $c_x ^ 2 = c_a c_x$ and $c_x c_y = 0$ if $x 
e y$. If $c_x = 0$ for all $x \in s$, then we are clearly done. Else find $x \in s$ such that $c_x 
e 0$. From the above two equations, we get that $c_x = c_a$ and $c_y = 0$ for all $y \in s, y 
e x$. Therefore \[c_x x = \sum_{y \in s} c_y y = c_a a = c_x a\] and $x = a$. Contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: adding a new group-like $a$ preserves independence

nodes.name: Assume $s$ independent and $a \notin s$ group-like
nodes.statement: Assume now that the finite set $s$ of group-like elements is linearly independent, that $a \notin s$ is group-like, and let's show that $s \cup \{a\}$ is linearly independent too.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $s$ independent and $a \notin s$ group-like

nodes.name: Apply $\Delta$ to a relation $\sum c_x x = c_a a$
nodes.statement: Assume there is some $c : A \to R$ such that $\sum_{x \in s} c_x x = c_a a$. Since $a$ and all elements of $s$ are group-like, we compute \begin{align*} \sum_{x, y \in s} c_x c_y x \otimes y & = c_a ^ 2 a \otimes a \\ & = c_a ^ 2 \Delta(a) \\ & = c_a \Delta\left(\sum_{x \in s} c_x x\right) \\ & = \sum_{x \in s} c_a c_x \Delta(x) \\ & = \sum_{x \in s} c_a c_x x \otimes x \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\Delta$ to a relation $\sum c_x x = c_a a$

nodes.name: Independence of $x \otimes y$ gives $c_x^2 = c_a c_x$ and $c_x c_y = 0
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{0-tensor-lin-indep}, the $x \otimes y$ are linearly independent and therefore $c_x ^ 2 = c_a c_x$ and $c_x c_y = 0$ if $x \ne y$.
nodes.statement_short: Independence of $x \otimes y$ gives $c_x^2 = c_a c_x$ and $c_x c_y = 0$

nodes.name: Case: all coefficients vanish
nodes.statement: If $c_x = 0$ for all $x \in s$, then we are clearly done.
nodes.statement_short: Case: all coefficients vanish

nodes.name: Otherwise $x = a$
nodes.statement: Else find $x \in s$ such that $c_x \ne 0$. From the above two equations, we get that $c_x = c_a$ and $c_y = 0$ for all $y \in s, y \ne x$. Therefore \[c_x x = \sum_{y \in s} c_y y = c_a a = c_x a\] and $x = a$. Contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise $x = a$, a contradiction

nodes.name: Group homs into group-likes extend to bialgebra homs
nodes.statement: If $f : G \to \GrpLike A$ is a group hom, then we get \begin{align*} R[G] \to A g \mapsto f(g) \end{align*} This is clearly an algebra hom, so for it to be a bialgebra hom we only need to check comultiplication is preserved. We only need to check this on $g \in G$, in which case \[(f \otimes f)(\Delta(g)) = (f \otimes f)(g \otimes g) = f(g) \otimes f(g) = \Delta(f(g))\] since $f(g) \in \GrpLike A$.
nodes.statement_short: Group homs into group-likes extend to bialgebra homs

nodes.name: Bialgebra homs restrict to group homs on group-like elements
nodes.statement: If $f : R[G] \to A$ is a bialgebra hom, then it restricts to a group hom $\GrpLike R[G] \to \GrpLike A$ by Proposition \ref{0-grp-like-map}. Now use that $\GrpLike R[G] \cong G$ from Proposition \ref{0-grp-like-grp-alg}.
nodes.statement_short: Bialgebra homs restrict to group homs on group-like elements

nodes.name: Reduce to checking generators
nodes.statement: It suffices to check the conditions of a Hopf ideal on generators.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to checking generators

nodes.name: Comultiplication condition
nodes.statement: For the comultiplication condition: \begin{align*} \Delta(h_1-h_2) &= \Delta(h_1) - \Delta(h_2) \\ &= h_1 \otimes h_1 - h_2 \otimes h_2 \\ &= h_1 \otimes h_1 - h_1 \otimes h_2 + h_1 \otimes h_2 - h_2 \otimes h_2 \\ &= h_1 \otimes (h_1 - h_2) + (h_1 - h_2) \otimes h_2 \in \bar{A \otimes I} + \bar{I \otimes A}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Comultiplication condition

nodes.name: Counit condition
nodes.statement: For the counit condition: \[ \varepsilon(h_1 - h_2) = \varepsilon(h_1) - \varepsilon(h_2) = 1 - 1 = 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Counit condition

nodes.name: Antipode condition
nodes.statement: Finally, for the antipode condition: \[ S(h_1 - h_2) = S(h_1) - S(h_2) = h_1^{-1} - h_2^{-1} \in I. \]
nodes.statement_short: Antipode condition

nodes.name: Factor $f$ through $R[f(G)]$
nodes.statement: Note that $R[G] \xrightarrow f A$ factors as $R[G] \xrightarrow f R[f(G)] \xrightarrow\phi A$, where $f(G)$ is a group by Proposition \ref{0-grp-like-grp}.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $f$ through $R[f(G)]$

nodes.name: The second factor is surjective
nodes.statement: Since $R[G] \xrightarrow f A$ is surjective, so is $R[f(G)] \xrightarrow\phi A$.
nodes.statement_short: The second factor is surjective

nodes.name: Apply the bijectivity criterion
nodes.statement: Therefore Proposition \ref{0-bialg-bij-of-span-grp-like} applies to $f(G)$ inside $A$, and we get $R[f(G)] \cong A$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the bijectivity criterion

nodes.name: Compose the two fully faithful functors
nodes.statement: Compose Propositions \ref{0-full-faithful-spec-hopf} and \ref{0-full-faithful-grp-alg}.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the two fully faithful functors

nodes.name: Pointers to Milne and SGA III for alternatives
nodes.statement: Also see Theorem 12.9(a) in \cite{Milne_2017}. See SGA III Exposé VIII for a proof that works for $R$ an arbitrary commutative ring.
nodes.statement_short: Pointers to Milne and SGA III for alternatives

nodes.name: The induced ring map $\Z[M] \to \Z[N]$ is surjective
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is surjective, the corresponding map $\hat f : \Z[M] \to \Z[N]$ is surjective too.
nodes.statement_short: The induced ring map $\Z[M] \to \Z[N]$ is surjective

nodes.name: Spec of a surjection is a closed embedding
nodes.statement: Hence $\Spec \hat f : \Spec \Z[N] \to \Spec \Z[M]$ is a closed embedding.
nodes.statement_short: Spec of a surjection is a closed embedding

nodes.name: Base change preserves closed embeddings
nodes.statement: Therefore $D_S(f)$ is a closed embedding, as closed embeddings are preserved under base change.
nodes.statement_short: Base change preserves closed embeddings

nodes.name: $H$ is affine
nodes.statement: $H$ is a closed subscheme of an affine scheme, hence it is affine.
nodes.statement_short: $H$ is affine

nodes.name: Write $H = \Spec A$ with $A$ a Hopf algebra
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{0-ess-image-spec-hopf}, write $H = \Spec A$ where $A$ is a $R$-Hopf algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Write $H = \Spec A$ with $A$ a Hopf algebra

nodes.name: The embedding becomes a surjection $R[G] \to A$
nodes.statement: The closed subgroup embedding $H \hookrightarrow D_R(G)$ becomes a surjective bialgebra hom $R[G] \to A$ by Propositions \ref{0-diag-spec} and \ref{0-full-faithful-spec-hopf}.
nodes.statement_short: The embedding becomes a surjection $R[G] \to A$

nodes.name: $A$ is diagonalisable
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{0-is-diag-bialg-quot}, $A$ is a diagonalisable bialgebra and therefore $H$ is a diagonalisable group scheme.
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is diagonalisable, hence so is $H$

nodes.name: Build an idempotent from a torsion element
nodes.statement: Say $x \in G$ is such that $x^n = 1$. Then \[e : R[G] := \frac 1n \sum_{i = 0}^n x^i\] is such that $e ^ 2 = e$.
nodes.statement_short: Build an idempotent from a torsion element

nodes.name: Conclude via $D_R(G) \cong \Spec R[G]$
nodes.statement: We are done by Proposition \ref{0-diag-spec}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude via $D_R(G) \cong \Spec R[G]$

nodes.name: Write $T \cong D_k(G)$ with $G$ free
nodes.statement: By assumption, write $T \cong D_k[G]$ for $G$ a free abelian group.
nodes.statement_short: Write $T \cong D_k(G)$ with $G$ free

nodes.name: $H \cong D_k(I)$ is diagonalisable
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{0-subgroup-diag}, $H$ is a diagonalisable group scheme, say $H \cong D_k(I)$ for $I$ an abelian group.
nodes.statement_short: $H \cong D_k(I)$ is diagonalisable

nodes.name: $G \to I$ surjective
nodes.statement: Since $H$ is a closed subscheme, the map $G \to I$ is surjective, so $I$ is a finitely-generated abelian group.
nodes.statement_short: $G \to I$ surjective, so $I$ finitely generated

nodes.name: Connectedness excludes torsion
nodes.statement: Since $H$ is connected, Proposition \ref{0-diag-tors} says $I$ is torsion-free, hence free.
nodes.statement_short: Connectedness excludes torsion, so $I$ is free

nodes.name: Conclude $H$ is a split torus
nodes.statement: Thus $H$ is a split torus.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $H$ is a split torus

nodes.name: The torus embedding comes from $M \hookrightarrow G$
nodes.statement: The map $D_k(G) \hookrightarrow D_k(M)$ is given by the embedding $M \hookrightarrow G$.
nodes.statement_short: The torus embedding comes from $M \hookrightarrow G$

nodes.name: Identify $D_k$ with Spec of monoid algebras
nodes.statement: We identify $D_k(G) \cong \Spec k[G], D_k(M) \cong \Spec k[M]$ using Proposition \ref{0-diag-spec}.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $D_k$ with Spec of monoid algebras

nodes.name: $k[G]$ is a localisation of $k[M]$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{0-loc-mon-alg}, $k[G]$ is a localization of $k[M]$. Therefore the map $\Spec k[G] \hookrightarrow \Spec k[M]$ is an open immersion.
nodes.statement_short: $k[G]$ is a localisation of $k[M]$, so the embedding is an open immersion

nodes.name: Dominance since $k[M]$ is a domain
nodes.statement: This open immersion is dominant since $\Spec k[M]$ is irreducible as $k[M]$ is a domain (Proposition \ref{0-aff-mon-alg-domain}).
nodes.statement_short: Dominance since $k[M]$ is a domain

nodes.name: The torus action is pulled back from the monoid action
nodes.statement: The group action $D_k(G) \times D_k(M) \to D_k(M)$ comes from pulling back along $D_k(G) \hookrightarrow D_k(M)$ the left action $D_k(M) \times D_k(M) \to D_k(M)$ using Proposition \ref{0-comap-mod}.
nodes.statement_short: The torus action is pulled back from the monoid action

nodes.name: Forward direction holds by definition
nodes.statement: A toric ideal is prime and generated by binomials by definition.
nodes.statement_short: Forward direction holds by definition

nodes.name: Converse: a prime binomial ideal is a lattice ideal
nodes.statement: Assume $I$ is prime and generated by $X^\alpha - X^\beta$ ranging over $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$ for some set $S \subseteq M \times M$. Note first that $I$ doesn't contain any monomial. Indeed, $I$ is contained in the kernel of the map $R[M] \to R$ given by $X^m \mapsto 1$. Since $I$ is prime, this means that \[ X^{\alpha + \gamma} - X^{\beta + \gamma} \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I. \] In particular, if $\alpha_1 - \beta_1 = \alpha_2 - \beta_2$, then Since $I$ is prime, this means that \[ X^{\alpha_1} - X^{\beta_1} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_1 + \beta_2} - X^{\beta_1 + \beta_2} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_2 + \beta_1} - X^{\beta_1 + \beta_2} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_2} - X^{\beta_2} \in I. \] Now, we claim that $I = I_L$ where $L \le G$ is given by \[ \Span\{\delta - \varepsilon | (\delta, \varepsilon) \in S\}. \] Clearly, $I \subseteq I_L$. For the other direction, assume $\delta, \varepsilon \in M, \delta - \varepsilon \in L$. Let's prove $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I$ by induction on $\delta - \varepsilon \in L$: \begin{itemize} \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = 0$, then $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon = 0 \in I$. \item If $\delta_1 - \varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 - \delta_2$ and $X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$, then \[ X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \in I \iff X^{\varepsilon_2} - X^{\delta_2} \iff X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = \alpha - \beta$ where $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$, then \[ X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item Assume $\delta_1, \delta_2, \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2$ are such that $X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1}, X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$. Then \[ X^{\delta_1 + \delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2} = (X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1})X^{\delta_2} + X^{\varepsilon_1}(X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2}) \in I. \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Converse: a prime binomial ideal is a lattice ideal

nodes.name: Take $I$ prime
nodes.statement: Assume $I$ is prime and generated by $X^\alpha - X^\beta$ ranging over $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$ for some set $S \subseteq M \times M$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $I$ prime, generated by binomials indexed by $S$

nodes.name: $I$ contains no monomial
nodes.statement: Note first that $I$ doesn't contain any monomial. Indeed, $I$ is contained in the kernel of the map $R[M] \to R$ given by $X^m \mapsto 1$.
nodes.statement_short: $I$ contains no monomial

nodes.name: Primality: binomial membership depends only on $\alpha - \beta$
nodes.statement: Since $I$ is prime, this means that \[ X^{\alpha + \gamma} - X^{\beta + \gamma} \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I. \] In particular, if $\alpha_1 - \beta_1 = \alpha_2 - \beta_2$, then Since $I$ is prime, this means that \[ X^{\alpha_1} - X^{\beta_1} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_1 + \beta_2} - X^{\beta_1 + \beta_2} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_2 + \beta_1} - X^{\beta_1 + \beta_2} \in I \iff X^{\alpha_2} - X^{\beta_2} \in I. \]
nodes.statement_short: Primality: binomial membership depends only on $\alpha - \beta$

nodes.name: Claim $I = I_L$
nodes.statement: Now, we claim that $I = I_L$ where $L \le G$ is given by \[ \Span\{\delta - \varepsilon | (\delta, \varepsilon) \in S\}. \] Clearly, $I \subseteq I_L$. For the other direction, assume $\delta, \varepsilon \in M, \delta - \varepsilon \in L$. Let's prove $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I$ by induction on $\delta - \varepsilon \in L$: \begin{itemize} \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = 0$, then $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon = 0 \in I$. \item If $\delta_1 - \varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 - \delta_2$ and $X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$, then \[ X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \in I \iff X^{\varepsilon_2} - X^{\delta_2} \iff X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = \alpha - \beta$ where $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$, then \[ X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item Assume $\delta_1, \delta_2, \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2$ are such that $X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1}, X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$. Then \[ X^{\delta_1 + \delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2} = (X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1})X^{\delta_2} + X^{\varepsilon_1}(X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2}) \in I. \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Claim $I = I_L$

nodes.name: $I \subseteq I_L$ is clear
nodes.statement: Clearly, $I \subseteq I_L$. For the other direction, assume $\delta, \varepsilon \in M, \delta - \varepsilon \in L$.
nodes.statement_short: $I \subseteq I_L$ is clear; take $\delta - \varepsilon \in L$

nodes.name: Induction on $\delta - \varepsilon \in L$
nodes.statement: Let's prove $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I$ by induction on $\delta - \varepsilon \in L$: \begin{itemize} \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = 0$, then $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon = 0 \in I$. \item If $\delta_1 - \varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 - \delta_2$ and $X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$, then \[ X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \in I \iff X^{\varepsilon_2} - X^{\delta_2} \iff X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item If $\delta - \varepsilon = \alpha - \beta$ where $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$, then \[ X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption. \item Assume $\delta_1, \delta_2, \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2$ are such that $X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1}, X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$. Then \[ X^{\delta_1 + \delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2} = (X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1})X^{\delta_2} + X^{\varepsilon_1}(X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2}) \in I. \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $\delta - \varepsilon \in L$

nodes.name: Zero case
nodes.statement: If $\delta - \varepsilon = 0$, then $X^\delta - X^\varepsilon = 0 \in I$.
nodes.statement_short: Zero case

nodes.name: Negation case
nodes.statement: If $\delta_1 - \varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 - \delta_2$ and $X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$, then \[ X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \in I \iff X^{\varepsilon_2} - X^{\delta_2} \iff X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1} \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Negation case

nodes.name: Generator case
nodes.statement: If $\delta - \varepsilon = \alpha - \beta$ where $(\alpha, \beta) \in S$, then \[ X^\delta - X^\varepsilon \in I \iff X^\alpha - X^\beta \in I \] by the remark, and this holds by assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Generator case

nodes.name: Sum case
nodes.statement: Assume $\delta_1, \delta_2, \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2$ are such that $X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1}, X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2} \in I$. Then \[ X^{\delta_1 + \delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2} = (X^{\delta_1} - X^{\varepsilon_1})X^{\delta_2} + X^{\varepsilon_1}(X^{\delta_2} - X^{\varepsilon_2}) \in I. \]
nodes.statement_short: Sum case

nodes.name: Torus $T'$ from the image-of-torus result
nodes.statement: {\textbf Torus: } Define the torus $T'$ to be the one we get from \ref{1-1-1-group-hom-torus} with quotient map $\pi:T \to T'$.
nodes.statement_short: Torus $T'$ from the image-of-torus result

nodes.name: Open embedding $T' \to Y_\MCA$
nodes.statement: {\textbf Open embedding: } Since both $Y_{\MCA},T'$ are closures of $\Phi,\Phi'$ and $\G_m^n\to\mathbb{A}^n$ is an open embedding we get an open embedding $\iota:T' \to Y_{\MCA}$ such that the map $\phi:T \to Y_{\MCA}$ factors as $\phi = \iota \circ \pi$.
nodes.statement_short: Open embedding $T' \to Y_\MCA$

nodes.name: Dominance
nodes.statement: {\textbf Dominant: } Since $\phi$ is dominant, so is $\iota$.
nodes.statement_short: Dominance

nodes.name: The $\G_m^n$ action restricts to $Y_\MCA$
nodes.statement: {\textbf Action: } Since $\G_m^n$ acts on $\mathbb{A}^n$, we get a morphism $a':T' \times_S Y_\MCA \to \mathbb{A}^n$. As $T'\times_S Y_\MCA$ is reduced (TODO add lemma), to show that this factors through $Y_\MCA$ it suffices to check that the image lies in $Y_\MCA$. First, $T'\times_S T' \to T'\times Y_\MCA$ is dominant, since $T'$ is flat and flat base change preserves dominance (TODO add lemma). Since the image of $T'\times_S T'$ is $T'$ we're done for topological reasons.
nodes.statement_short: The $\G_m^n$ action restricts to $Y_\MCA$

nodes.name: Equivariance of the torus inclusion
nodes.statement: {\textbf Equivariant: } The inclusion of the torus is equivariant, since $\G_m^n \to \mathbb{A}^n$ is.
nodes.statement_short: Equivariance of the torus inclusion
